title: What Zen is not
hook: not just calm, not just paradox: a whole way with ethics, ritual and community

segments.voice: The week closes. A stone bridge that lets donkeys cross. The question what is this. Three months in a Korean retreat. Sitting and chanting in Vietnam. A Chan hall full again. And yesterday, a last poem. What made it into your four lines? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-three.
screen: `DONKEYS CROSS.` · `WHAT IS THIS.` · `THREE MONTHS IN.` · `A LAST POEM.`

segments.voice: A scented candle with the word zen on the label. A tea called zen. A spa, a phone app, a paint color, all promising zen. In everyday English the word has come to mean relaxed, unbothered, nothing getting to you. Meanwhile, in a Zen temple, the day may begin before dawn with bowing and chanting. People recite vows together. The floors get scrubbed. A meal is eaten from a set of bowls in a set order. And the teacher expects everyone to keep the precepts. Calm may be in there somewhere. It isn't the whole picture. Today: what Zen is not.
screen: `ZEN ON A CANDLE LABEL.` → `BOWING, CHANTING, SCRUBBING.` → `WHAT ZEN IS NOT.`

segments.voice: First, Zen is not just calm. Calm can come from sitting, and nobody turns it away. But look where this block kept pointing. The herdsman rides home and then walks back into the market. The meal is eaten from nested bowls, just enough, and every bowl cleaned. Zen points at seeing clearly, and seeing clearly includes the moments that aren't calm at all. Second, Zen is not just paradox. Koans like the stone bridge or three pounds of flax get passed around for their strangeness. But a koan lives inside a relationship: a student, a teacher, a meeting room, many hours on the cushion. Pulled out alone, it looks like a riddle. Inside the practice, it's work. Third, ethics. Zen communities hold a ceremony for receiving the precepts, called jukai in Japanese. People vow not to kill, not to steal, not to lie, and more. The precepts are the floor the cushion sits on. An old verse in the Dhammapada puts the whole path in one line. In Max Müller's translation: "Not to commit any sin, to do good, and to purify one's mind, that is the teaching of (all) the Awakened." Notice the order. Purifying the mind comes last, after not harming and doing good. Fourth, ritual and community. Bowing, chanting, robes, bells, shared meals, people who sit beside each other week after week. Strip those away and what's left is the word on the candle. Keep them, and Zen is a whole way of living with other people, with sitting at its center.
screen: `NOT JUST CALM.` · `NOT JUST PARADOX.` · `THE PRECEPTS UNDER THE CUSHION.` · `RITUAL AND COMMUNITY.` · then, large: `MORE THAN CALM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. Choose one precept to keep for the rest of today. Not killing, which might mean carrying a spider outside instead of swatting it. Not stealing, which might mean not taking credit or time that isn't yours. Not lying, which might mean no small, easy untruths, even the polite ones. Pick just one. Then sit with it, the way someone receiving precepts might: breathing in, breathing out, holding the choice quietly. The bell holds the time.
What Zen is not: not only calm, and not only paradox. A whole way, with precepts, ritual and community, and sitting at its center. Today's word.

Your line: more than calm. Today, when you hear zen used to mean relaxed, remember the precepts, the bowing, and the people side by side in the hall. And keep the one precept you chose. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: Zen communities keep the precepts alongside sitting: in a ceremony called jukai in Japanese, practitioners formally receive vows such as not killing, not stealing and not lying, and daily life in a Zen temple includes bowing, chanting, work and meals taken together.
